b1026a52: How many calories to eat to lose weight: estimate your TDEE, pick a 300–500 calorie deficit, and adjust with real data. A practical step-by-step guide.
5700c997: "Eat less, move more" is technically correct and practically useless. The number that actually matters is your daily calorie target — and most people are guessing at it, often by a margin wide enough to explain why the scale won't move.
5908286f: Start with maintenance, not a diet number
441ac265: Before you can eat in a deficit, you need to know what "even" looks like — the number of calories that keeps your weight stable. This is your Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE): your body's baseline burn (BMR) plus everything you do on top of it — walking, workouts, fidgeting, digestion.
45cc0852: A common starting formula for BMR is Mifflin-St Jeor:
aee26de9: Men: (10 × weight in kg) + (6.25 × height in cm) − (5 × age) + 5
aff63e96: Women: (10 × weight in kg) + (6.25 × height in cm) − (5 × age) − 161
07a97764: Multiply that BMR by an activity factor — roughly 1.2 for sedentary, 1.375 for light activity a few days a week, up to 1.55 or higher for regular training — and you get a workable TDEE estimate. It won't be exact. Nobody's is. It's a starting point you correct using real data, which is the part most people skip.
25e57026: The deficit size that actually sticks
14374a8a: One pound of body fat is roughly 3,500 calories. That math tempts people into aggressive deficits — cut 1,000 calories a day, lose two pounds a week. In practice, deficits that large are hard to sustain, tend to cost more muscle than fat, and usually end in a binge that erases the week's progress.
11f45482: A deficit of 300–500 calories per day is small enough to hold for months and large enough to show up on the scale within two to three weeks.
c59a3b7b: That pace works out to roughly 0.5–1 lb (0.25–0.45 kg) of weight loss per week for most people — slow enough to preserve muscle and energy levels, fast enough to stay motivating.
0b0757d0: Why your estimate needs a feedback loop
f2d7f93e: Here's the part formulas can't do: TDEE calculators are a guess, not a measurement. Metabolism varies by more than the equations account for, and it shifts as you lose weight — a lighter body burns less at rest and in motion. The only way to know your real number is to track intake consistently for two to three weeks and compare it against what the scale actually does.
9652f9ed: Weight stayed flat? That intake is close to your true maintenance — your deficit starts from there.
5415fb9b: Weight dropped faster than expected? Your real TDEE is lower than estimated — small, common, easy to adjust for.
e7e0a54f: Weight didn't move at all on a "deficit"? Almost always a logging gap, not a broken metabolism.
173b9a4c: That last point is the one that sinks most attempts. Manual food diaries undercount by a wide margin — a bite here, a splash of oil there, a forgotten handful of nuts — and those small misses compound over a week into a very different number than the one you logged.

3371600d: How to track calories at restaurants: order smart, estimate portions, and log meals you didn't cook without guessing wildly or skipping the entry.
14b2d33e: Restaurants are where most tracking attempts quietly fall apart — not because the food is worse, but because there's no nutrition label on the table. Here's how to order, estimate, and log a restaurant meal without either guessing wildly or skipping the log entirely.
ee115ee2: The order matters more than the tracking
f53da50b: The biggest lever you have at a restaurant isn't your logging accuracy — it's what you order before any of that starts. A grilled protein with a starch and a vegetable side is close to home-cooked in macro terms. A dish described as "loaded," "crispy," or "smothered" usually means it's carrying calories in the preparation, not just the ingredients.
5e71dcd3: You don't need to eat differently at a restaurant. You need to order the version of the meal that isn't hiding calories in the cooking method.
6ef4b266: Four menu words worth reading twice
5756dec6: Almost always fried or coated in a way that roughly doubles the fat content versus a grilled or roasted version of the same protein.
ec8e9809: Signals a dairy- or mayo-based sauce added on top — often 200-400 extra calories that don't show up in the dish's name.
2e71d35f: A salad's calorie count usually lives in the dressing, not the vegetables. Asking for it on the side is one of the highest-leverage requests you can make.
055165b1: Portion sizes at restaurants routinely run 1.5-2x a standard serving — worth mentally splitting before you start eating, not after.
ab639646: You don't need the exact number — you need a defensible estimate
a69a0b21: Perfection isn't available when someone else cooked the meal. What's available is a reasonable estimate, logged consistently, which beats a perfect number logged occasionally. A few habits that get you close:
87a89e5d: Log before you eat, not after. Committing to an estimate before the plate arrives keeps you from anchoring to how full you feel afterward, which has nothing to do with the actual calorie count.
1199363d: Round up on sauces and oil. Restaurant kitchens are far more generous with both than a home kitchen — when in doubt, assume more, not less.
4fbe6b40: Use the closest match, not the exact dish. A dish that isn't in any database is still close enough to "grilled chicken, rice, vegetables" for tracking purposes.

9b86baaf: What Is a Food Health Score? How It's Calculated | PlateAI
8a38a0eb: Why two meals with identical calories can score very differently: how a food health score weighs macro balance, nutrient density, and portion signals.
14b19983: Two meals can have identical calories and completely different health scores — which confuses people the first time they see it. That gap is the entire point. Calories tell you about energy; they don't tell you much about what a meal is actually made of.
6acc34b2: It's not a calorie count wearing a different label
93cf776c: A 500-calorie plate of grilled salmon, greens, and quinoa is not nutritionally interchangeable with a 500-calorie serving of fries and a soda, even though your calorie total for the day would look identical either way. The health score exists to surface that difference — a single number that reflects the quality of a meal, not just its energy content.
f5da4819: Calories answer "how much energy." The health score answers "how well does this meal serve the rest of your body."
d9508df1: What actually goes into the number
5b7d04bd: The score blends several signals from the same analysis that generates your macros, weighted toward what the evidence on diet quality consistently points to:
0127b4ad: Balance across protein, carbs, and fat
18103344: A plate isn't scored on being "low-carb" or "low-fat" in isolation — it's scored on whether the macro mix is reasonably balanced for a single meal, rather than dominated by one macro at the expense of the others.
b1768e50: Density of fiber, vitamins, and minerals
bf49d193: Two meals with the same calories can differ enormously in fiber and micronutrient content. Whole, minimally processed ingredients tend to score higher here than refined or heavily processed ones.
8f05966c: Plate coverage and apparent portion size feed into the estimate — a reasonable serving reads differently than one that visibly overshoots a typical meal.
c4c24421: Why it's a relative signal, not a grade
e5dfa26b: The most useful way to read the health score is comparatively — across your own meals, over time — rather than as a pass/fail grade on any single plate. A 6 today and an 8 tomorrow tells you something real about the shift in what you ate. A 6 in isolation doesn't mean you did something wrong; the occasional lower-scoring meal is normal and expected. It's the pattern across a week that's worth paying attention to, the same way the weight trend line matters more than any single day.
67c6fa47: The score arrives after your macros, not instead of them
43a780ab: It's stage three of PlateAI's analysis — core macros land first, the health score follows once the fuller nutrient picture is in.
29a97cce: None of this replaces judgment — a score is a compressed signal, not a verdict. But when you're deciding between two lunch options and the calories look about the same, it's the fastest way to see which one is actually doing more for you.
ed6a310a: The health score is a general wellness indicator generated from photo analysis and is not a substitute for professional dietary or medical advice.

f223a438: Halo foods get a pass they haven't earned
fcac085f: Researchers call this the "health halo" effect — when a food is labeled or perceived as healthy, people consistently underestimate its calorie content and eat larger portions of it without noticing. It's not a willpower problem. It's that "healthy" and "low-calorie" got merged into the same idea in most people's heads, and they're not the same thing at all.
1ecbd87b: Nutrient-dense and calorie-dense aren't opposites. Plenty of foods are both at once — and those are exactly the ones worth double-checking.

9f447a22: Calorically dense by design — a "spoonful" often runs closer to double that.

cd0e33c0: How to Calculate Your Macros for Weight Loss | PlateAI
ef0ba047: How to calculate macros for weight loss: set calories, then protein, fat, and carbs by bodyweight. Includes a worked example and gram targets by weight.
da7a7de8: Most macro calculators hand you a split like 40/30/30 and call it a day. The trouble is that percentages hide what actually matters: how many grams of protein you're getting, and whether your fat is low enough to hurt. Here's a simple way to calculate macros for weight loss that starts from your bodyweight instead.
f2991a0d: What are macros, and why track them?
38a20c7a: Macros — short for macronutrients — are the three nutrients that supply your calories: protein, carbohydrate, and fat. Calories set whether you lose weight. Macros shape what you lose (fat versus muscle), how full you feel, and how well you train.
8baba210: If you're new to tracking, start with our beginner's guide on how to count calories first — macros build directly on top of it.
515a79b4: Everything else is carved out of this number. Estimate your maintenance calories (TDEE), then subtract about 300–500 kcal for steady weight loss. If you haven't done that yet, our guide to how many calories to eat to lose weight walks through it. For the examples below, we'll use a 160 lb (73 kg) person eating 1,800 kcal a day.
cfe0bbb3: Protein comes first because it's the macro with the most to gain from being set deliberately. In a calorie deficit, a higher intake helps preserve muscle and keeps hunger manageable. A practical range is 1.6–2.2 g per kg of bodyweight (about 0.7–1.0 g per lb) — see how much protein you need per day for the reasoning.
4714c548: For our example we'll use 0.8 g per lb: 160 × 0.8 = 128 g of protein. Protein has 4 calories per gram, so that's 512 kcal.
7bb86fad: Fat is calorie-dense (9 kcal per gram), so it's easy to overshoot — but going too low backfires. Fat helps you absorb vitamins A, D, E, and K and makes meals more satisfying. A sensible target for most people is roughly 0.3–0.45 g per lb of bodyweight, which usually lands between 20% and 35% of total calories.
bc02fe69: For our example, 0.35 g per lb: 160 × 0.35 = 56 g of fat, or 504 kcal.
3d48f76b: Step 4: Let carbs fill the rest
e9099175: Carbohydrates are the flexible macro. Whatever calories remain after protein and fat go to carbs, at 4 kcal per gram:
dcb0318a: 1,800 kcal − 512 (protein) − 504 (fat) = 784 kcal ÷ 4 = about 196 g of carbs.
51004a86: That gives a final target of roughly 128 g protein / 56 g fat / 196 g carbs — about 28% protein, 28% fat, and 44% carbs. Carbs fuel training, so if you lift or run regularly, this is the macro you want to protect.
30d964dd: Using the same method (0.8 g protein and 0.35 g fat per lb, carbs fill the remainder), here are approximate starting points at a few sizes. Round freely — these are starting points, not prescriptions.
a8451a91: Hitting the numbers is the hard part
3dec5871: PlateAI shows your calories, protein, carbs, and fat against your daily goals from a single photo — so you know by lunch what dinner needs to cover.
cb78fb1f: A "40/30/30" split sounds precise, but percentages move with your calories. At 1,400 kcal, 30% protein is 105 g; at 2,800 kcal, it's 210 g — the same percentage, wildly different amounts. Setting protein and fat by bodyweight keeps the things your body actually needs stable, and lets carbs flex with your calorie target and activity.
f45ce01c: Chasing perfect ratios. Landing within about 10% of your protein target on most days matters far more than hitting an exact split every day.
637c2f6f: Cutting fat too low. Going under the range above can leave you hungry and unsatisfied without speeding anything up.
adb349a5: Slashing carbs by default. Low-carb can work for some people, but cutting carbs too far often hurts training and adherence. Calories still decide weight loss.
e0c1897d: Forgetting fiber. Aim for roughly 25–35 g a day from vegetables, fruit, legumes, and whole grains. It helps fullness and digestion.
f51bce32: Overlooking hidden fat. Oils, dressings, and cooking fats are easy to miss — see healthy foods that are surprisingly high in calories.
a3538b29: How to adjust your macros over time
061256f3: Treat your first set of numbers as a draft. Track consistently for two to three weeks, then look at your weekly average weight, not a single morning's reading — our guide on how often to weigh yourself explains why. If the trend is flat despite consistent logging, trim about 100–150 calories, mostly from carbs or fat, and keep protein where it is. If energy or training tanks, add a little back.
1b2fbce7: Eating out or logging meals you didn't cook? A close estimate is fine — see how to track calories and macros when eating out.
3a4ac3a1: What is the best macro split for weight loss?
5cd6ad0a: There isn't a single best split. What matters most is a calorie deficit you can sustain and enough protein. A common starting point is around 25–35% protein, 25–35% fat, and the rest carbs, but setting protein and fat by bodyweight, as above, is more reliable.
a702739b: Do I need to hit my macros exactly?
fb3e5d61: No. Aim to be within roughly 10% of your protein and calorie targets on most days. Weekly averages matter more than any single day.
7b60eeea: Are macros or calories more important for weight loss?
fd229d84: Calories determine whether you lose weight; macros influence how it goes — muscle retention, hunger, and performance. Get calories right first, then protein, then fine-tune the rest.
8907436b: Should I track macros or just protein?
26786b78: If tracking everything feels like too much, tracking calories and protein alone captures most of the benefit. Add carbs and fat once that feels automatic.
a73615c3: How many carbs should I eat to lose weight?
94693bf8: It depends on your calorie target and activity level. Carbs are what's left after protein and fat are set, which for many people falls between about 100 and 300 g a day.

90f686c9: Set protein at roughly 0.7–1.0 g per lb of bodyweight.
fdb84414: Set fat at roughly 0.3–0.45 g per lb.
cb3e0aa2: Fill the remaining calories with carbs (4 kcal per gram).
afb6e418: Review your weekly average after two to three weeks and adjust.

e2c195a0: How to count calories for beginners: set a target, choose a logging method, avoid hidden-calorie mistakes, and track without a food scale. Step by step.
1521666b: Counting calories is one of the most reliable ways to lose weight, gain muscle, or just understand what you eat — and one of the easiest things to quit in the first week. Almost always that's because the method was too fiddly, not because you did anything wrong. Here's a beginner-friendly system that takes minutes a day.
43f8cdfb: A calorie is a unit of energy. Food gives you calories; your body spends them on everything from breathing to running. If you eat about what you spend, your weight holds steady. Eat consistently less and it trends down; eat more and it trends up. Counting calories is just keeping a running tally of what goes in, so you can compare it with a target.
bbec1dcb: That's the whole idea. Everything below is about doing it with as little friction as possible — because the plan you actually keep doing beats the perfect one you drop after ten days.
4faa908c: Step 1: Set a daily calorie target
fc8fb4e3: You need a number to count against. Start by estimating your maintenance calories (your Total Daily Energy Expenditure, or TDEE) with an online calculator or the Mifflin-St Jeor formula, then adjust for your goal:
0c8401fd: Lose weight: eat roughly 300–500 calories below maintenance.
5b250957: Build muscle: eat roughly 200–300 calories above maintenance.
669afc69: Example: if your estimated maintenance is 2,200 kcal and you want to lose weight steadily, a starting target of about 1,800 kcal is reasonable. Treat it as a first draft, not a verdict — we cover how to refine it with real data in our guide on how many calories to eat to lose weight.

bccdd420: Does intermittent fasting work for weight loss? What the evidence says about 16:8 and time-restricted eating, and why the window matters less than you think.
d14e168d: Intermittent fasting gets talked about like it has some metabolic trick that regular eating doesn't. It mostly doesn't — and understanding why is more useful than the trend itself, because it tells you whether the 16:8 window is actually going to help you personally.
ae6fa76c: The mechanism is simpler than the hype
22530e0c: Most popular intermittent fasting research compares time-restricted eating (commonly a 16-hour fast, 8-hour eating window) against unrestricted eating for weight loss. When both groups end up eating the same total calories, the weight loss results come out roughly the same. The fasting window isn't burning extra fat through some separate mechanism — it's mainly working by making it harder to eat as much.
bba4a397: Intermittent fasting isn't a metabolic hack. It's a calorie-deficit tool that happens to work by shrinking the number of hours you can eat in.
2f55d2e9: Skipping breakfast removes one full meal's worth of choices and temptations from the day — for some people that's a real reduction in how often willpower gets tested.
63717761: Some people genuinely aren't hungry in the morning and have been eating breakfast out of habit — for them, an eating window just matches what their appetite was already doing.
3bc5a60e: "Don't eat before noon" is easier to follow consistently for some people than tracking every meal — the simplicity itself is the benefit, not the fasting physiology.
a4031329: Compressing all your food into a shorter window makes it easier to eat past fullness in that window — a large percentage of "I'm doing 16:8" reports involve two very large meals that roughly offset the calories saved by skipping breakfast. It also front-loads hunger and irritability for people who don't adapt well to it, which shows up as worse workouts, worse sleep, or a binge later in the week.
7bb785f4: If you're someone who trains early, needs steady energy through the morning, or finds that skipping breakfast makes you overeat later, fasting isn't fixing anything for you — it's just moving the same challenge to a different part of the day.

922d8dab: If a fasting window makes staying in a deficit easier for you personally, keep it. If it makes you ravenous and prone to overeating later, it's not the right tool for you — and that's a completely normal outcome, not a failure.

7db41537: The commonly cited 0.8 g of protein per kilogram of bodyweight (about 0.36 g per pound) is the U.S. RDA — the minimum intake to prevent deficiency in a sedentary adult. 026e68d8: 1.6–2.2 g of protein per kg of bodyweight (roughly 0.7–1.0 g per pound) covers nearly everyone from "generally active" to "training seriously," with higher end reserved for a calorie deficit.
dec025a6: Why protein needs go up when calories go down
b565d94e: This is the part most calorie-counting advice misses entirely. In a deficit, your body is looking for energy anywhere it can find it — and without enough protein coming in, some of that energy comes from muscle tissue, not just fat. f56659e0: Protein also carries the highest satiety value of the three macros — gram for gram, it keeps you fuller longer than carbs or fat, which matters enormously when you're eating in a deficit and hunger is working against you.

74749d54: Learn to estimate calories from a photo of food: the visual cues that carry real signal — sheen, char marks, plate coverage — and where to gut-check.
0d98dd69: Before any AI touched a photo of food, dietitians were already doing visual estimation — sizing up a plate by eye and landing surprisingly close to the real numbers. The trick isn't magic. It's knowing which visual cues actually carry information, and which ones are misleading.
ca9f0dc2: Plate coverage is the first, roughest signal
425503d8: How much of the plate is covered, and how high the food is piled, gives a rough read on total volume — the starting point for any estimate. But volume alone is a weak signal on its own: a cup of leafy greens and a cup of rice occupy similar space and carry wildly different calorie counts. Coverage sets the ballpark; everything else refines it.
9a1a123e: The visual cues that matter most aren't about size — they're about what's coating the food.
f1a3492d: A visible sheen on food is almost always oil, butter, or sauce — and fat is the most calorie-dense macro by a wide margin. A dry-looking piece of chicken and a glossy one can differ by 100+ calories despite looking like "the same food."
ba3c3bbe: Grill marks, deep browning, or a crisped edge usually signal a cooking method that added fat (pan-searing, frying) rather than a drier method like steaming or boiling — and can hint at breading or a sugar-based glaze.
980e090c: Pooling at the base of the plate
c95c8a68: Sauce or oil pooled around food is a strong signal that the visible portion isn't the whole story — there's often more fat or sodium sitting under or around what you can clearly see.
23346359: A fork, a standard plate edge, or a hand in frame gives a scale reference that makes portion estimates meaningfully more accurate than a tight, context-free crop of just the food.
569119c0: Where photo estimates still need a gut-check
405261f2: Visual analysis is genuinely good at reading what's on the surface — but it can't see what's mixed into a dish. A stir-fry with oil tossed through it before plating, a soup with cream stirred in, or a salad dressed and mixed before serving all hide their fat and calorie content below what the eye (or a model) can directly observe. In those cases, an estimate is a solid starting point, not a certainty — and it's worth adjusting manually if you know what went into the pan.

0fecef5b: Body weight can swing 2–4 lb (1–2 kg) in a single day from things that have nothing to do with fat gain or loss: sodium intake, carb intake (each gram of stored carbohydrate holds roughly 3g of water), hydration status, hormonal cycles, how recently you ate, and even how well you slept. 9109f15e: A single weigh-in is a data point. A trend line built from 7–14 days of weigh-ins is information.
f53c6762: Water weight releasing — not "1.5 lb of fat lost"
6a0316a5: Both of those readings are real. Neither one, on its own, tells you anything about whether you're actually losing fat. The trend across two weeks does.

4f22896e: PlateAI's Weight Control reminder defaults to a weekly check-in (Monday mornings) instead of a daily one, and that's a deliberate choice, not a missing feature. 8e40fdb8: A weekly cadence, taken under consistent conditions (same time of day, ideally after waking and before eating), naturally averages out most of the daily noise without you having to do any math.

55e49e4c: Never react to a single day. Look at a 7-day rolling average, not yesterday's reading.
8279d9bd: Weigh under the same conditions — same time, same state of dress, ideally after using the bathroom and before eating or drinking.
1fbe05d1: Judge progress in two-to-three week windows. One week of "no movement" is normal variance, not a stalled plan.
